growing up i had a friend i used to visit just to play on  his Gameboy, this was early 2000, not really sure but i think it was the original Game Boy, the one that ran on an 8bit chip barely past 4MHz, we played tetris and supermario land back then, good times.

got the nostalgia trying to draft a summary listening back to Rituals AMA the other day,
 
@ArshanKhanifar said the ethereum virtual machine, the thing every smart contract on ethereum actually runs inside of, is less powerful than that Game Boy...

sounds overboard but, take a deep dive into the setup Arshan gave.

the EVM is deliberately tiny. programs you submit to it (contracts) used to be capped around 32kb, recently bumped up a bit but still small. and everything it does has to be deterministic, meaning the exact same input has to produce the exact same output, every single time, on every single node, forever. 

that's not a limitation nobody thought about, it's the entire point. thousands of validators have to independently compute the same state and agree on it, and the only way that works is if there's zero room for variation.

which is fine, until you try to put AI anywhere near it.

ethereum actually saw a version of this coming too.

there's a standard called ERC-8004, "trustless agents," put together by davide crapis and a few others at the ethereum foundation..

the thinking behind it is simple once you strip it down, agents are going to be transacting with other agents they've never met, built by companies and platforms with nothing to do with each other, so there needs to be some shared, neutral place where an agent can prove who it is and show a track record of behaving honestly. 

8004 gives you three registries for exactly that, identity, reputation, and validation, basically an immutable public record any agent can check before deciding whether to trust another agent it just met.

that's a real problem and ethereum's answer to it makes sense given what ethereum actually is. it's not trying to run the agent's thinking, it's trying to be more like a paper trail that thinking can point back to..

but that's also exactly where it stops short, a spotless identity and a flawless reputation trail doesn't mean much if the agent behind it can just get switched off.

the registry doesn't go anywhere, it just sits there as a record of an agent that used to exist. 8004 answers who do i trust. it doesn't answer where does this thing actually live and how does it keep thinking, and that second question is the one that decides whether there's still an agent standing behind the reputation by the time anyone goes looking for it. 

that's basically niraj's design argument from earlier in the call, just showing up again from a different angle.

 you can join identity and reputation onto a chain that was never built to run the intelligence itself, and it'll work, right up until whatever server sits behind it goes down.

or you can build the chain so the intelligence, the memory, and the keys never had to live off it in the first place. thats ritual.

and 8004 just shows that even ethereum agrees the problem is very real.

you can ask a model the same question twice, you'll get two different answers, I've seen a lot of people post this of late, you can as well try it yourself,  

none of that is a bug in the model or the oracle, it's just what non deterministic computation actually is. and blockchains, by design, cannot natively agree on something that isn't guaranteed to come out the same way twice.

this is the actual wall, the consensus math underneath every chain assumes a kind of computation that AI doesn't do.

ritual's answer to this is something Arshan called EOVMT, execute once, verify many times, and with they way he explained it i couldn't unsee it everywhere in the design

Great news - the AI Act has led to the emergence of a brand-new market! In the past few weeks, tools capable of removing watermarks from AI-generated content have seen a huge increase in popularity. Even though the AI Act appears to be moving in the right direction, as I pointed out recently, the EU still lacks initiatives that actively support its local market. Regulations by themselves aren't sufficient. The only exception appears to be tools designed to erase their very consequences 😉.

Here is a breakdown of what this arms race looks like:

1. To ensure the provenance of AI-generated materials, multiple independent security measures are being used, with companies adopting a multi-layered method that involves both obvious, cryptographically signed metadata - such as that specified by the C2PA standard - and statistical changes at the level of token selection in texts or in the frequency structure of pixels in images.

2. Rather surprisingly, text watermarking tools have no effect on perplexity. Since perplexity indicates how well a language model is able to produce text - the lower the perplexity, the better the model is at predicting the next word in a sentence - this suggests that the text seems more natural, and at the same time implies that the model has more extensive knowledge and is able to generate better responses to prompts.

3. The pressure from regulators to keep track of content provenance has led to a swift reaction among developers. Tools for removing watermarks are becoming increasingly popular. A good example is the GitHub repository watermarks-remover. Just a few days after Anthropic announced its new model safeguards, it obtained more than 10,000 stars. This increase clearly shows a strong demand for systems aimed at hiding the origin of artificial intelligence.

4. Although GitHub tools easily deal with metadata, when it comes to combating token watermarking, they use brute-force approaches such as having the text rewritten by another model. Research has shown that meaning-preserving attacks, such as multiple back-translations, greatly decrease the detectability of watermarks.

In the case of images the matter is a great deal more complicated. Libraries are now setting up machine learning-based procedures for eliminating pixel alterations, but the encoders that apply these pixels are trained in an adversarial manner to be as resistant to removal as possible. It therefore follows that noise strong enough to destroy such a watermark usually causes serious visual deterioration of the image itself.

5. The imposition of watermarks has deeply divided experts, with the discussions pointing to a fundamental clash between theoretical cybersecurity and the practical usability of AI systems. It is undoubtedly a significant advance to introduce permanent safeguards since this enhances accountability and makes it much easier to combat harmful disinformation.

Nevertheless, practice leads to unpleasant side effects for all. Nowadays, these safeguards are built directly into the fundamental predictive structure of language models. Even a brief use of an AI network - such as merely correcting a few commas - results in a permanent artificial signature being added to the whole file. In the end, this will set up major obstacles for scientists and creators, greatly complicating the development of multilingual content.

All of this is a fundamental misunderstanding of how AI generation actually works. This would have been true 7 or 8 years ago. All of this is entirely out of date. I'll explain it to you, but you probably wont understand it.

The image synthesis architectures of Grok’s Aurora, OpenAI’s DALL·E 3, and Google’s Imagen 3 (Nano Banana) instantiate distinct generative paradigms within the broader class of foundation-model-driven multimodal diffusion and autoregressive transformers. Aurora implements a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) autoregressive transformer pretrained on interleaved text-image corpora; upon ingestion of the tokenized prompt embedding, it performs sequential next-token prediction over a discrete visual codebook, generating raster-ordered patches via expert-gated feed-forward layers conditioned solely on prior tokens and prompt cross-attention, followed by a lightweight decoder that maps the completed token lattice through a variational autoencoder (VAE) to high-resolution RGB pixel space. DALL·E 3 first employs a GPT-4o backbone for prompt distillation into a richly conditioned CLIP/T5-style text embedding; this drives a latent diffusion model initialized from isotropic Gaussian noise in the compressed VAE latent manifold, where a U-Net or diffusion transformer (DiT) iteratively subtracts predicted noise residuals across a fixed denoising schedule, injecting multimodal guidance via cross-attention at each timestep before final VAE upsampling to full-resolution output. Imagen 3, natively fused with Gemini’s multimodal encoder-decoder, executes a cascaded diffusion pipeline: a base latent diffusion transformer establishes global scene layout at low resolution from random noise, succeeded by successive super-resolution diffusion stages that progressively refine high-frequency detail, text legibility, and photometric fidelity through hierarchical noise prediction and prompt-conditioned self-attention, with an embedded SynthID watermark injected in the final latent-to-pixel decoding.
Collectively, these systems operationalize the end-to-end transduction of natural-language conditioning vectors into photorealistic raster imagery via either autoregressive token-by-token assembly or stochastic Langevin dynamics in latent space, executed on distributed GPU/TPU inference clusters optimized for low-latency sampling. Prompt embeddings serve as fixed conditioning signals throughout the forward pass, enabling zero-shot adherence to user intent while post-hoc safety classifiers and minimal artifact-suppression filters ensure policy-compliant output; the resultant pipeline thereby achieves seamless conversational image co-generation without exogenous artistic priors, exemplifying the scaling laws that govern emergent cross-modal synthesis in contemporary large-scale generative AI.

Technology can be potentially* positively transformative. But don't let them conflate all machine learning with the generative AI products forced upon, devolving, and destroying the world. Public opinion often can't separate tech from products they know it as. This doesn't require an endless landscape of data centers. Even some gen AI has legitimate use, but none of it (even at its maximal potential) is worth its monumental costs.

* The asterisk on "potentially" is because society today is fundamentally built on exploitation, so tech can't be allowed to actually ease labor burdens in some utopic fashion, only benefit employers (usually by saving them money) and thrust those newly unemployed by the tech back into poverty and even more exploitable with their skillsets devalued.

Also, tech increasingly isn't allowed to be disruptive of traditional capital centers (e.g. industries). Historically, inventions have disrupted industries because discoveries were somewhat accessible to the common man. But, tech has become so advanced that further invention requires concerted effort with specialized equipment, environments, manpower, and knowledge bases exclusive to those that hold the capital!

And obviously, corporations don't want disruption. So infinite opportunities to better the world with our most incredible capabilities as a species pass by day after day to focus on reinforcing what already is. And right now, what is is not great. Another fundamental problem with capitalism. Don't mess with the capital, even when it would be in the best interest of everyone.

MEET THE AI GIRL WHO PLAYS TENNIS FOR A LIVING — AND SHE'S NEVER LOST

She trains, competes, and racks up wins on camera. The catch: she doesn't exist.

Here's how the "AI athlete" model actually works:

An AI girl persona is built with a consistent face, body, and personality using image/video generation tools. Instead of lifestyle or fashion content, her niche is sport — match highlights, training vlogs, "behind the scenes" prep, rackets and outfits, rivalries with other AI athletes.

The mechanism is simple: physical talent doesn't need to be real, only the narrative around it does. Generated match clips, fake tournament brackets, and AI commentary create a storyline fans follow like a real career.

How she earns:

Sponsorship deals with sportswear/equipment brands looking for cheap, controllable "athletes"
Paid fan subscriptions for exclusive training content and match reactions
Licensing her face/likeness to sports betting or fantasy-sim apps
Selling a personal "AI coach" app trained on her persona
NFT/collectible drops tied to her "career milestones" (Grand Slam wins, rankings)

The twist: her fanbase doesn't care that she's never held a racket — they're not following an athlete, they're following a story that updates on schedule
